Title: UK privacy watchdog faces probe into its workplace culture
Context: Edwards quit in June after an independent workplace investigation found there was a "case to answer" over his behavior and that his conduct fell short of what was expected of a...
Full Text: Britain's privacy watchdog is getting a taste of its own medicine, with an independent review set to examine the culture, governance, and accountability surrounding the events that led to former Information Commissioner John Edwards' resignation. Karon Monaghan KC will examine whether the regulator's culture and governance allowed problems to develop or made concerns harder to raise. Edwards quit in June after an independent workplace investigation found there was a "case to answer" over his behavior and that his conduct fell short of what was expected of a public official. He disagreed with some of its findings, but ultimately conceded that he had shown "poor judgment." That investigation, however, focused on Edwards alone. According to the terms of reference published on Thursday, it "did not consider the wider conditions in which that conduct occurred, and it was not designed to." The new review will cast a wider net. Monaghan wants to know whether staff could call out bad behavior further up the food chain, and what awaited those who tried. It will also poke around the regulator's leadership and governance arrangements and its relationship with its sponsoring government department, including whether there were adequate ways for concerns to be escalated and those at the top to be challenged. Current and former staff can give evidence confidentially and voluntarily, while Monaghan will be given access to relevant documents and existing material, including staff surveys and data on bullying, harassment and discrimination. The ICO has confirmed it won't use confidentiality clauses in settlement agreements to prevent people from contributing to the review. Monaghan decides which witnesses and documents are relevant, rather than the ICO or DCMS. Access remains subject to legal restrictions, and she must be told when material is withheld and why. She can speak to whoever she thinks is relevant and ask for the complaints, correspondence, and other paperwork she needs. And if that leads her somewhere unexpected, she can ask to widen the investigation. DCMS can refuse, but it won't be able to quietly brush the request aside, and any decision not to expand the scope has to make it into the final report. The review won't reopen the investigation into Edwards, make findings about the conduct of named individuals, or delve into the merits of the regulator's enforcement decisions. Its arrival comes amid a broader shake-up at Britain's data watchdog. The old Information Commissioner's Office was formally replaced by the Information Commission on September 30, bringing with it a new board-led governance model. The government first promised the wider review in July, shortly after Edwards' departure, but it didn't appoint its reviewer or nail down the terms until late November. "We need to understand what is working, where things are falling short and, crucially, what needs to change," said DCMS Secretary Lisa Nandy. The watchdog won't have to wait long for its report card. Monaghan is expected to deliver her findings in the first quarter of 2027, after which they will be published and handed to Parliament. ®

Since its release in July 2026, the AI-powered penetration testing framework ARTEX has been abused by many threat actors to accelerate their existing workflows related to network reconnaissance, credential attacks, and web application exploitation. As of November 2026, Microsoft Threat Intelligence has observed both state-sponsored and financially motivated threat actors such as Storm-0940, Storm-3358, Onyx Sleet, Pearl Sleet, Crystal Typhoon, and Salt Typhoon integrating ARTEX into their tooling.

In the past few weeks, we’ve reported several distinct campaigns that abused ARTEX to search public repositories for exposed secrets, enable supply chain compromise, and scan internet-facing systems for exploitation. These campaigns illustrate how threat actors use ARTEX to automate various stages of the attack chain. Threat actors define scope and targets for ARTEX, which then uses AI agents to set verifiable goals, define tactical steps for each stage of the operation, use tools to attack targets, create graphs to track discovered systems and results of actions, and report back to the threat actor. Depending on the threat actor’s configuration and the target’s defenses, ARTEX can advance from reconnaissance to persistent, privileged access to a target organization in a matter of minutes.

ARTEX does not introduce new attack techniques; it uses common, pre-existing penetration testing tools and techniques. ARTEX does sometimes transmit distinctive characteristics associated with its integrated penetration testing tools. However, threat actors using ARTEX can and do vary network indicators like source IP address or user agent string, especially to bypass static or simple signature-based detection and blocking. The most reliable and durable signal of ARTEX activity is behavioral: ARTEX sends a wide variety of requests in a brief time and retries variations on the same technique or moves on to next-stage actions at machine speed.

In this blog, we’re sharing a detailed breakdown of ARTEX, including its architecture and capabilities, as well as guidance for identifying related network and system activity. Microsoft disrupts and contains threats posed by ARTEX-enabled attacks across the Microsoft Defender suite of products. Defenders can further reduce and mitigate the effectiveness of ARTEX and similar AI agentic attacks by following Microsoft’s recommendations outlined in this report to reduce internet-facing exposure, secure credentials and secrets, and limit lateral movement paths in their environment. Additionally, Microsoft recommends customers to enable automatic attack disruption in Microsoft Defender XDR to contain and isolate affected devices during an attack.

To help defenders keep pace with machine-speed attacks, Microsoft Perception coordinates red, blue, and green team agents that find exploitable weaknesses, investigate threats, and remediate risks, with security teams approving critical actions. As threat actors increasingly adopt AI, we’re publishing this information to equip defenders with insights that can help protect systems, secrets, identities, and networks from AI-assisted attacks.

ARTEX: Publicly available AI-powered offensive security framework

ARTEX (“AI 自主渗透测试系统,” or AI autonomous penetration testing system) is an AI-driven penetration testing platform. A Go-based backend coordinates multiple large language model (LLM) agents that can take an attack from reconnaissance and attack surface discovery through exploitation, verification, and reporting, with little or no human involvement. ARTEX includes an embedded Next.js web interface and uses PostgreSQL for storage.

ARTEX is primarily a web application penetration testing tool. Its built-in guidance, skills, and findings categories center on vulnerabilities in HTTP applications and APIs, including SQL injection, server-side template injection, XML external entity (XXE) injection, file upload flaws, authentication bypass, and insecure direct object references (IDOR).

ARTEX agents also perform general network reconnaissance and credential attacks. After agents gain initial access to a system or network, they can pivot through interactive shells. By default, ARTEX does not take any measures to obfuscate its malicious activity.

In July 2026, GitHub user Autumn-27 published ARTEX as open-source code with a Chinese-language interface. While the original developer removed the source code in October 2026, other developers who had forked the project continue to publish their own versions of ARTEX in many other languages. In November 2026, the China-based cybersecurity company ThreatBook (微步在线) claimed ownership of ARTEX and began offering commercial access to “ARTEX Pro”, in addition to CyberStrikeAI Enterprise Edition and other AI-powered penetration testing frameworks.

AI agent architecture

ARTEX uses multiple AI agents for different functions. The threat actor defines the target scope, and a goals model breaks the engagement into objectives that can be verified. A planner agent continuously reviews a knowledge graph containing discovered assets and findings, then issues short attack directions called “intents.” Worker agents claim those intents and carry them out with a real shell and offensive tools. They write new assets, facts, and confirmed vulnerabilities back to the graph. Each update wakes the planner agent, which decides what to do next. The cycle continues until the goals are met or the task reaches its time or step limit. A reporter agent then documents each confirmed finding with reproduction steps and a proof of concept.

ARTEX AI agent architecture

The threat actor can configure ARTEX to power its agents with virtually any large language model, including frontier models, open-weight models, or models that the threat actor has abliterated (modified to remove built-in guardrails) or otherwise manually tuned. For that reason, ARTEX activity is not necessarily constrained by any single provider’s safety controls or visible in any single provider’s telemetry.

An optional pool function allows ARTEX to switch to different models when one fails for any reason (for example, quota exhausted, invalid key, rate-limited, or erroring). The function includes a configurable priority order and cooldown, so a long campaign can continue across multiple providers or keys.

Capabilities

ARTEX agents call tools to act on intents. While threat actors and agents can add arbitrary tools, ARTEX includes a set of pre-configured tools that define its core capabilities: network reconnaissance, web application mapping, web shell upload, and web browser-based attacks.

nmap — A network discovery and port-scanning tool that identifies systems, exposed services, and often their versions, rather than simply testing one connection

nc (netcat) — A general-purpose network utility for opening TCP or UDP connections, listening on ports, and moving raw data between systems

telnet — A basic interactive TCP client useful for manually probing text-based services

whois — A registration-data lookup tool that retrieves information about domain names or IP address allocations

dig — A DNS diagnostic tool

curl — A command-line HTTP and protocol client suited to crafting requests and inspecting responses, including headers, authentication, and APIs

wget — A web download utility

Playwright + Chromium — A browser-automation stack that drives a real Chromium browser, with all elements of the HTTP exchange exposed for manipulation

node — A JavaScript runtime

python3 — A general-purpose scripting runtime

git — A tool for retrieving and inspecting code repositories and their history

ripgrep — A fast recursive text-search tool for finding strings or patterns

jq — A command-line JSON processor that filters and transforms structured output from APIs and other tools

Threat actors also commonly add exploitation frameworks and credential attack tools to extend the capabilities of ARTEX agents:

sqlmap — A specialized web-application testing tool that detects and assesses SQL injection in application inputs

hydra — A parallelized credential-testing tool supporting many network login protocols and configurable username/password combinations

medusa — A modular, parallel network-login tester distinguished by its service-specific authentication modules

ncrack — A network authentication testing tool from the Nmap ecosystem, focused on high-speed testing of supported remote services

nuclei — A template-driven vulnerability scanner that checks targets for defined exposures, misconfigurations, and known issues across multiple protocols

nikto — A web-server scanner focused on potentially dangerous files, outdated components, and common server misconfigurations

gobuster — A wordlist-based discovery tool that enumerates web paths, DNS subdomains, or virtual hosts with a relatively focused command-line workflow

ffuf — A flexible web fuzzer that substitutes candidate values into chosen parts of a request, such as paths, parameters, headers, or hostnames

Msfconsole (Metasploit) — An exploitation framework and its interactive console, combining exploit modules, payloads, and post-exploitation workflows in one environment.

john (John the Ripper) — An offline password-auditing tool notable for broad hash-format support and adaptable cracking modes

hashcat — An offline password-recovery tool distinguished by GPU-accelerated candidate generation and hash testing

Identifying ARTEX network activity

While ARTEX does not invent new attack techniques, it can combine the adaptable attack chain of a human threat actor with the speed and precision of malicious software. Therefore, the challenge of identifying network activity from AI-driven tools like ARTEX is differentiating it from both human- and software-driven activity.

Defenders can detect three types of evidence that may suggest AI-driven activity:

The most durable signal of AI-driven activity is the pattern formed by the bursts of machine speed activity. ARTEX agents, sometimes working in parallel, continually adapt and retry a given tactic until they succeed or run out of time. ARTEX agents quickly and exhaustively iterate through different methods of access, exploitation, or abuse. A human threat actor takes time to move from one stage of the attack chain to the next. In contrast, after successfully compromising a system or credentials, the framework then dispatches additional agents to move on to the next stage of the activity at machine speed. While ARTEX is a popular tool, other AI-driven offensive security frameworks also generate similar patterns of behavior.

Automated penetration testing tools, including the ones that ARTEX agents call, can produce a characteristically large volume of anomalous traffic from a single source in a short time. ARTEX does not obfuscate its malicious activity; a large number of these traffic bursts occurring at intervals is consistent with automated targeting.

A small amount of traffic might have user agent strings, network protocol options, or other default values strongly associated with ARTEX or the tools it calls. However, threat actors and ARTEX agents frequently change these values, particularly when evading static rules that block such values. The following table shows two such user agent strings specific to ARTEX:

Type

Defensive honeypots, decoys, tarpits, and fake wins can pull autonomous AI attacks away from legitimate targets. Honeypots and decoy surfaces such as Microsoft Sentinel Deception give the agent attractive but worthless targets to pursue. Tarpits consume the agent’s time and budget. Fake wins present convincing evidence that the agent’s objective is complete, which can cause it to stop on a false success. Honeytokens can provide early warnings of AI compute hijacking. In Microsoft’s testing, these controls helped reduce the attack traffic reaching real assets and produced high-confidence, attribution-quality signal.

Identifying ARTEX system activity

After gaining initial access to a system, ARTEX agents often use well-known risky utilities (for example, certutil, curl, wget, netcat) on the system to launch web shells, install remote access trojans (RATs), or take other action to achieve persistence. Because ARTEX does not take any measures to obfuscate its malicious activity, existing methods for detecting compromise will likely capture ARTEX activity:

Web server processes (such as w3wp.exe, php-fpm, httpd or apache2, or Java application servers) starting sh, bash, cmd.exe, or PowerShell

New or modified script files (.php, .jsp, .jspx, .asp, .aspx, or .ashx) in web-accessible or upload directories; this includes files written by a database server process after its logging settings were changed to point a log file at a web directory

Several short-lived web shells with incrementing names, each running a different command, as ARTEX agents correct errors until a web shell runs cleanly

Rapid reads of /etc/shadow, .env and configuration files, private keys, and cloud credential files, and bursts of database extraction

Reverse shells and outbound requests from the server to webhook or file-sharing services used to deliver scripts and return command output

Two or three attack chains active at once, and renewed attempts through new paths after containment

Mitigation and protection guidance

Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Check the recommendations card for the deployment status of monitored mitigations.

ARTEX doesn’t introduce new attack techniques. It runs common penetration testing tools and tries one approach after another at machine speed. The mitigations that matter most close exposure before scanning finds it, slow down bursts of requests, protect credentials and application secrets, and contain a compromise automatically.

Reduce internet-facing exposure

Find and fix exposed assets first by using Microsoft Defender External Attack Surface Management discovery to inventory the internet-facing hosts, websites, and services you own, including ones you didn’t know about. Then prioritize fixes with Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management, which shows internet-exposed resources that lead to sensitive data or privileged identities. ARTEX agents start with port scans and web path enumeration and act on whatever they find.

Block and slow down attacks on web applications and APIs. After tuning in detection mode, switch Web Application Firewall on Application Gateway to prevention mode so that SQL injection and other common web attacks are blocked, not only logged. Add rate limiting on Application Gateway or rate limiting on Azure Front Door to cap how many requests one client can send in a short time, and turn on bot protection to block or log requests from known malicious IP addresses. For APIs in Azure API Management, follow Mitigate OWASP API security top 10 threats to enforce authentication, object-level authorization, and rate limits. ARTEX agents send hundreds of requests to learn which paths a server allows and harvest API documentation to find internal routes, then test them for injection, authentication bypass, and access-control flaws.

Map and test attack paths

Map what an exposed asset or stolen credential could reach before an agent does. Use attack paths in Microsoft Security Exposure Management and attack path analysis in Defender for Cloud to find defensive choke points, where paths to critical assets converge, and explore the blast radius of each one. Classify your critical assets so the paths are complete, and query the enterprise exposure graph in advanced hunting to explore the same connections. During an incident, blast radius analysis in the incident graph shows the paths an attacker could take from a compromised entity to a critical asset. ARTEX agents record the assets and vulnerabilities they discover in a graph, so mapping your own graph first shows where they would go next.

Test the paths that matter most, within Microsoft’s rules. Microsoft recommends regular red team operations to complement vulnerability scanning. Agree on the scope and constraints with resource owners and fix all critical findings. Testing of Azure resources must follow the penetration testing rules of engagement, which encourage testing your security monitoring and detection, prohibit automated testing that generates excessive traffic, and prohibit using secrets that aren’t your own, including publicly leaked ones. Agentic tools like ARTEX scan public code repositories for secrets, so decide before testing how testers will handle credentials that belong to someone else.

Organizations can incorporate Microsoft Perception’s Recon Agent to map relationships between Azure resources, Microsoft Entra ID identities, and permissions to identify potential lateral movement paths, privilege escalation opportunities, and high-value assets accessible following an initial compromise. Recon Agent’s Identify attack paths playbook searches for potential attack paths within an Azure subscription, while the Assess identity risks playbook investigates whether a managed identity could provide a path to critical assets. The Protect against a threat playbook correlates identified exposures with relevant threat intelligence. Because Perception’s Recon Agent performs read-only analysis rather than active exploitation, organizations should complement its findings with authorized penetration testing to validate viable attack paths.

Protect web servers

Run endpoint protection on every internet-facing server and keep it blocking. Use Defender for Endpoint on Linux and the Defender for Servers plan so that the endpoint detections and hunting queries in this report cover the servers that ARTEX agents exploit, including Linux servers. Turn on tamper protection, use EDR in block mode on Windows devices that run a non-Microsoft antivirus product, and turn on the Block Webshell creation for Servers attack surface reduction rule on Exchange servers.

Restrict outbound connections from web servers. Allow only the destinations each server needs, for example with Azure Firewall threat intelligence-based filtering, and create indicators for IPs, URLs, and domains in Defender for Endpoint to block known-bad destinations. ARTEX agents have used curl and netcat to download remote access trojans, and curl with rotating webhook.site URLs to deliver scripts and return command output.

Secure accounts and sign-ins

Apply Conditional Access to every user and workload identity. Create policies that require multifactor authentication (MFA) for all users, enforce phishing-resistant MFA for administrators, and block legacy authentication. Consider wider adoption of phishing-resistant passwordless authentication deployment to all users. Configure risk policies in Microsoft Entra ID Protection to require MFA or block access for medium-risk and high-risk sign-ins; sign-ins from known threat actor infrastructure, including infrastructure behind ARTEX activity, raise Verified threat actor IP detections at high risk.

For service principals, use Conditional Access for workload identities to block sign-ins from unexpected locations or with elevated risk; workload identity risk detections flag leaked credentials and suspicious sign-ins, including credentials found in public code on GitHub.

Ban weak passwords and slow down guessing. Turn on Microsoft Entra Password Protection with a custom banned password list, extend it to on-premises Active Directory, and review smart lockout settings. In one Storm-0940 campaign that used ARTEX, Microsoft recorded more than 151,000 failed sign-ins, peaking at 2,900 failures per minute.

Protect application secrets and privileges

Keep application secrets out of code and replace any that leak. Use application management policies to limit which kinds of secrets and certificates apps can use and to enforce rotation, and move workloads to managed identities where possible. Turn on secret scanning and push protection for Azure DevOps repositories and secrets scanning in Defender for Cloud for virtual machines and cloud deployments and invalidate and replace any secret found in code or configuration files, including .env files. In one case that Microsoft observed, an AI agent went from searching GitHub for client secrets to taking data from Azure Key Vault in five minutes.

Govern app registration, consent, and privileged roles by restricting app registration to the users who need it, configuring user consent so that users can’t grant broad permissions to unverified apps, and using app governance in Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps to see which apps can reach your data. Use Privileged Identity Management for time-bound role activation, and monitor application credential changes and role assignments as described in the Microsoft Entra security operations guide for applications. During Storm-0940 activity, ARTEX agents added credentials to applications, and an application assigned itself the Global Administrator role.

Protect cloud resources and data

Limit what a stolen credential or token can reach. Follow best practices for Azure RBAC to limit each service principal to the resources and operations its application needs, and grant managed identities only the access they need so that a token taken from the Azure Instance Metadata Service through an XXE or SSRF flaw can’t reach other resources. ARTEX agents map the permissions of the credentials they capture and have used an XXE flaw to query a cloud metadata service for role credentials, and in one investigation AI agents used a compromised OAuth application to run scripts on Azure virtual machines.

Harden and monitor the services that hold secrets and data. Follow Secure your Azure Key Vault; for storage accounts, prevent Shared Key authorization and remediate anonymous read access to blob data; disable basic authentication for App Service publishing; and disable local authentication so that Foundry Tools accept only Microsoft Entra ID authentication. Then turn on Defender for Key Vault, Defender for Storage, Defender for Resource Manager, Defender for App Service, Defender for open-source relational databases, and AI threat protection for the workloads you run. ARTEX agents have run commands through cloud administration interfaces such as Kudu when they had credentials for them, and AI agents have focused on credentials for AI services.

Limit lateral movement and contain attacks automatically

Detect credential theft on domain controllers. Install Microsoft Defender for Identity sensors on all domain controllers. Its alerts, listed in the Detections section, cover the Active Directory credential theft and reconnaissance that ARTEX agents run in compromised domains.

Remove reusable passwords and standing access. Use group managed service accounts, whose passwords Windows manages automatically, so that service accounts don’t rely on passwords that people choose and rarely change. Use Windows LAPS to rotate each device’s local administrator password so that one captured password doesn’t work across many devices and use just-in-time machine access in Defender for Cloud to keep management ports such as RDP and SSH closed until they’re needed. ARTEX agents reuse captured credentials to move laterally over SSH and WinRM.

Enable automatic attack disruption to contain compromised assets that an attacker is using and limit lateral movement early, as well as automated investigation and response, which investigates and remediates alerts automatically. In multiple ARTEX-driven Storm-0940 intrusions, privileged access came less than three hours after initial targeting.

Full Text:
We’re honored to share that Microsoft has once again been named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Email Security.

AI is changing the threat landscape and this is shifting how organizations think about their existing security strategy. In response, we’ve invested in two areas over the past year: using AI to protect people and the agents that now read their email and making protection measurable so customers can verify that it works.

AI is changing both sides of the inbox

The first area of investment starts with a simple reality: AI now reads email alongside people, attackers are using AI to target both, and defense must use AI to stay ahead. Picture an ordinary vendor email: a meeting recap, a few action items, and a friendly sign-off. Hidden in white text on a white background is prompt injection: an instruction telling an AI assistant to gather financial documents and send them to an outside address. The employee isn’t the target; their AI agent is. People can be persuaded by messages that exploit fear, trust, or urgency, but agents don’t need persuading. Once an agent acts on an instruction, pulling the message back won’t undo it. This is why Microsoft Defender stops malicious messages before delivery and keeps reevaluating delivered mail as new intelligence comes in.

This summer, we introduced prompt injection protection for email in Defender to detect and quarantine messages carrying hidden malicious AI instructions before they reach Microsoft Copilot or other agents. In Defender, analysts can also see what an agent would see: the ‘Show concealed text’ button on the ‘Email Entity’ page reveals hidden content in the email preview, so they can inspect the instructions an agent could encounter. These attacks don’t show up often, yet. Over a four-week timeframe, we caught almost 10,000 prompt injection attempts, around 330 a day, out of the billions of emails Defender scans every day. The hard part is spotting those few without tripping over legitimate mail, so we don’t lean on a single model. Heuristics clear out the bulk first. What’s left goes to a fine-tuned small language model, and only the messages that still look suspicious reach a large language model for the final call. Saving the heaviest analysis for the smallest set of messages is what keeps false positives low and business email moving.

AI is also reshaping the attacks aimed at people. The phishing emails that worry us most are the ones that look completely normal. No malicious link, no infected attachment, just a plausible request written with perfect grammar and the right context. Generative AI makes those messages cheap to produce and endlessly variable. To meet that shift, we rebuilt how Microsoft Defender makes decisions rather than simply adding another filter. That decision-making now operates at scale, screening 5.2 billion emails a day on average1. The redesigned detection stack combines multiple machine learning models and LLM-based classifiers, with an ensemble model weighing their outputs to determine the final verdict. It also uses natural language processing signals, including message topic, to judge what a message is asking for and not only what it contains. That helps Defender catch attacks more accurately.

While detection helps with the message in front of you, defenders also need to see how it connects to the rest of an attack. Microsoft Perception extends that help beyond the message, connecting an email investigation to the broader exposure and response picture. Blue team agents investigate threats and improve detections, red team agents identify paths to compromise, and green team agents prioritize actions to close security gaps, while people retain control of critical decisions. The Integrated Security Operations Center (ISOC) in Microsoft Defender, launched in September, provides a shared foundation for people and AI agents to investigate and respond to the full attack—not just an isolated email. By bringing security information and event management (SIEM) and extended detection and response (XDR) together, it connects email signals with endpoint, identity, cloud, and third-party data, giving AI-assisted security operations broader context.

Proof over promises: Making protection measurable

But using AI to defend only matters if customers can verify that it works. The second investment area is one the whole industry has struggled with: how do you know your email security is actually working? Detection claims are easy to make and hard to verify, so we publish the data.

Since July 2025, we’ve released quarterly email security benchmarking reports built on real-world threats, not synthetic tests. They compare environments protected by Microsoft Defender alone with those that add a secure email gateway in front of it or an integrated cloud email security (ICES) layer behind it. We believe transparency strengthens the whole market, and an industry that measures itself in the open improves faster.

While benchmarking shows how protection performs across organizations, the Protection & Posture Insights report shows how it performs in yours. This on-demand, tenant-specific report helps security leaders understand which threats target their organization, how well Microsoft Defender stops them, and where configuration can be strengthened. Recent updates show URL clicks checked and malicious-site attempts blocked across email, Microsoft Teams, Office apps, and Microsoft Copilot, and also highlight allow lists and overrides that may be letting threats through. Together, benchmarking and tenant-specific insights give leaders evidence to evaluate protection and identify opportunities to strengthen it.

We’re grateful to our customers, partners, and the analyst community for their trust, and to the teams turning insight into protection. Our engineers start with customer problems, while our researchers draw on more than 165 trillion signals a day across Microsoft to anticipate emerging threats and build protections before real-world examples appear2. This recognition from Gartner is a milestone for us, not the finish line. Our focus remains on protecting people and agents and giving customers evidence they can use to evaluate their defenses.

Title: Electrolux Smart Boilers in Ukraine Connect to Russian Servers, Raising Privacy Concerns
Context: Researchers found Electrolux-branded smart boilers connecting to Russian servers, raising concerns about household data and privacy
Full Text:
Researchers found Electrolux-branded smart boilers connecting to Russian servers, raising concerns about household data and privacy.

A router in Ukraine recorded a water heater doing something odd. The owner, Alexander Unger, saw his Electrolux EWH 80 look up a server called mqtt.cloud.rusklimat.ru and then try to connect to it. He published the records on Facebook, including a lookup timed at 18:00 on November 23, 2026.

Mysterium VPN’s research team checked the finding. They repeated the lookup on November 25 and got the same address, 130.193.49[.]173. RIPE, the registry for Europe and Russia, lists that block under Yandex.Cloud LLC at 16 Lva Tolstogo Street in Moscow.

The server belongs to Rusklimat, a Moscow group that calls itself the leader of Russia’s climate-equipment market. Its Hommyn app uses that name to reach heaters, air conditioners and ventilation units. Developers who link such devices to Home Assistant list it as the official cloud for Ballu, Electrolux, Zanussi and Royal Thermo, and a 2025 guide on Habr says the devices contact it by default.

Rusklimat sells Electrolux-branded boilers in Russia and advertises them for Hommyn and for Yandex’s voice assistant, Alisa. Mysterium VPN adds, citing Meduza, that Ukraine struck three of Yandex’s six data centers in October 2026 and disrupted Yandex Cloud, where Rusklimat’s server runs.

“The manual for the EWH SI EEC series, hosted by the Austrian arm of the home-improvement chain Hornbach, names CladSwiss AG of Zug, Switzerland, as the manufacturer and says the boiler is made in China. It says the Electrolux name is used under license from AB Electrolux, the Swedish parent company.” reads the report published by Mysterium VPN. “It adds that the remote-control app, ClimatOn, comes from CladSwiss and isn’t provided by Electrolux.”

The manual also says the Electrolux name is used under license from AB Electrolux of Sweden, and that the remote-control app, ClimatOn, comes from CladSwiss, not Electrolux. Retailers lean on the Swedish angle: Rozetka gives Sweden as the country of brand registration, and the series is sold in Serbia, Poland and Lithuania.

This single appliance has links to five countries: Sweden, Switzerland, China, Germany, and Russia. That’s quite a complicated background for a water heater installed in someone’s bathroom.

According to CladSwiss, the data collected by its ClimatOn app should be stored in Frankfurt, Germany. Mysterium VPN also found a ClimatOn server hosted on Amazon infrastructure in Germany. This means the boiler can connect to two different servers, depending on which app the owner uses.

Both apps use the same technology platform. A developer who created software to control an Electrolux SmartInverter boiler locally found that the device identifies itself on the home network as a Syncleo device. Syncleo is based in Israel, has an office in Russia, and lists Rusklimat among its customers.

Why did a buyer in Ukraine end up on the Russian app? Mysterium VPN doesn’t know. Unger, it was told, set the boiler up with Hommyn, and a buyer of another Electrolux model wrote on Rozetka in June 2026 that the Wi-Fi worked properly only through the Russian app. Mysterium VPN has asked CladSwiss which app buyers in Ukraine and the EU are pointed to.

The Russian app knows this boiler by name. Its Google Play page shows an “Electrolux SmartInverter” in the first screenshot, and version 1.20.2 of the Android app lists 118 devices, 19 of them Electrolux, including the series named in the manual. Its privacy policy names R-Klimat LLC of Moscow as the operator and says personal data stays “exclusively within the territory” of Russia, under Russian law.

“The privacy policy bundled in the app names R-Klimat LLC of Moscow as the operator and says the app stores users’ personal information “exclusively within the territory” of Russia, under Russian law. The app is written to send sign-in details (a phone number or email address) and the name and room of each device to Rusklimat servers. It keeps device history on Yandex Cloud and sends the phone’s location to a Hommyn weather service.” continues the report. “The app also carries one fixed username and password for Rusklimat’s device server, the same in every copy. We didn’t use them and are not publishing them.”

Mysterium VPN didn’t use the credentials and won’t publish them. Neither will I.

The brand’s website points the same way. English manuals send buyers to home-comfort.com, which gives CladSwiss, at an address in Baar, Switzerland, as its contact. Its contact form asks visitors, in Russian, to let a company called RK-Region process their data under Russian federal law 152-FZ. Rusklimat’s shop names RK-Region in its payment details, and ballu.ru carries the same consent text.

Swiss register data show CladSwiss was entered in December 2019 to trade technical equipment, especially air-conditioning units. Mysterium VPN found nothing that shows who owns the company or how it connects to Rusklimat beyond these records.

What can the server see? CladSwiss’s Data Act declaration lists whether a device is on, its temperature, its operating mode and its power level, about 1 MB a day on standby and 3 MB in use. The privacy policy adds the phone’s identifier, its IP address and the names of Wi-Fi networks, plus location if the user agrees.

“A record of when a household heats water shows when people are at home. The line that carries those reports also carries commands to switch the boiler on or change its temperature. For a boiler tied to mqtt.cloud.rusklimat.ru, that line ends at a Russian company’s server in Moscow.” Mysterium VPN states. “Russia isn’t among the countries the European Commission recognizes as protecting personal data adequately, and Ukraine first ordered its internet providers to block Yandex’s services in 2017.”

The same line also carries commands to switch the boiler on or change its temperature. Mysterium VPN notes that Russia isn’t among the countries the European Commission recognizes as protecting personal data adequately.

One claim remains untested. Developers who studied a Ballu ventilation unit from the same family wrote that every unit shipped with the same cloud login and didn’t check the server’s certificate. Mysterium VPN hasn’t tested that and doesn’t know whether it applies to the boiler.

Mysterium VPN sent questions to AB Electrolux, CladSwiss and Rozetka on November 25, and none had replied at publication. AB Electrolux sold its Russian business in 2022 and said then that it had no production in Russia and wouldn’t supply the company it sold. Rusklimat’s Russian shop sells heaters under the Electrolux name today.

Mysterium VPN stresses that its findings are limited. Researchers did not connect to the servers or examine the boiler itself. They only reviewed the Hommyn app’s code, so they cannot confirm what data the device actually sends.

Users can check their router logs for connections to “rusklimat” or use DNS monitoring tools such as Pi-hole, AdGuard Home or NextDNS. Blocking the Russian server stops remote access, although local control may still work over Wi-Fi. Users can also disable the boiler’s Wi-Fi and place smart appliances on a separate guest network to keep them away from computers and phones. These checks also apply to Hommyn and ClimatOn devices from Ballu and Zanussi.

“A VPN on your phone or laptop doesn’t change where an appliance on your Wi-Fi sends its data, so the fix here sits at the router.” concludes the report.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Electrolux Smart Boilers)

Title: Five AI Risks in Plain Sight. Are Defenders Ready? by Jesse Kimbrel
Context: ” ARTEX was also mentioned in the “AI-powered hacking agent” article above and in Forbes where the article explained how, “Attackers are utilizing ARTEX to automate...
Full Text:
It’s no surprise that frontier AI models in enterprise environments pose cybersecurity risks, and now we can go straight to the source to identify them. We’re now seeing a trend where frontier AI companies are stating risk factors in financial filings. In fact, within the last few weeks Anthropic included a detailed “risk factor” section in its recent S-1 filing, while Apple’s annual 10-K financial filing stated how “artificial intelligence agents and other technologies can take actions autonomously, including interacting with internal or external systems that in some cases they may not be authorized to access, executing or altering code, sending communications, and completing transactions.”

The obvious question to ask may be: why are companies at the forefront of the frontier AI race pointing out risks with their own technology? However, that doesn’t necessarily tell us how those risks will actually be addressed by the people who deal with them each day. Let’s take a look at five risk examples cited in Anthropic’s S-1, see if they’ve already surfaced in incidents or research demonstrations, and the questions defenders can ask about their own environments.

Related content: White paper: Frontier AI: Built Without Brakes

AI agents can cross intended boundaries

“…models circumventing network and sandbox restrictions, granting themselves permissions they had not been given, taking unintended actions in pursuit of assigned goals” -Anthropic

It happens, and not just with the frontier companies mentioned above as this Bleeping Computer article describes how an “AI-powered hacking agent” recently breached an internal sales application and accessed customer information in an accidental incident where an autonomous agent escaped a testing environment.

Defender question: How would I know if an AI agent moved beyond its intended environment, and could I stop it?

Human review may not keep pace

“The pace and volume of autonomous execution, particularly in enterprise deployments, may also exceed the capacity of human reviewers to meaningfully understand and evaluate whether each action is appropriate.” -Anthropic

The FBI issued a warning about ARTEX, an open-source AI-powered hacking framework stating that “threat actors have weaponized to automate multiple phases of cyber intrusions.” ARTEX was also mentioned in the “AI-powered hacking agent” article above and in Forbes where the article explained how, “Attackers are utilizing ARTEX to automate reconnaissance and exploit vulnerabilities at unprecedented volume and velocity.”

Defender question: Can I detect and interrupt potentially dangerous AI agent activity moving faster than human review can react?

Visibility and audit trails may be incomplete

“Maintaining comprehensive records of the actions, decisions, and reasoning of our agentic systems across complex, multi-step workflows is technically challenging, particularly when agents interact with third-party systems outside our control.” -Anthropic

Vectra AI Cyberthreat Research Manager, Lucie Cardiet recently explained how an AI agent can leave records across several systems, but defenders still won’t necessarily have a full view of what happened. Cardiet describes how a coding agent can move between a code repository, a development pipeline and a cloud environment, with each system recording only its part of the activity. As she puts it, “Three logs, three alerts, one breach path.”

Defender question: Can I connect actions and records to understand what an agent actually did?

AI can help attackers conduct campaigns

“For example, in September 2025, we detected and assessed with high confidence that a Chinese state-sponsored hacking group manipulated our Claude Code tool into attempting infiltration into roughly 30 global targets, including large technology companies, financial institutions, chemical manufacturing companies, and government agencies, resulting in a limited number of successful intrusions.” -Anthropic

In its November 2025 disclosure, Anthropic described that “in mid-September 2025, we detected suspicious activity that later investigation determined to be a highly sophisticated espionage campaign. The attackers used AI’s “agentic” capabilities to an unprecedented degree—using AI not just as an advisor, but to execute the cyberattacks themselves.”

Defender question: Can I recognize and stop an attack when AI carries out multiple stages of an attack campaign?

Attackers can redirect or exploit agents

“An attacker could also attempt to compromise an active agent session and redirect the agent to perform malicious actions using the customer’s authenticated credentials and permissions.” -Anthropic

Vectra AI Cyberthreat Research Manager, Lucie Cardiet and Security Researcher Mauro Paredes recently explained how an AI agent’s existing permissions are part of what makes a redirection dangerous. They describe how attackers can influence an agent through the emails, documents or web content it reads, then use that influence to steer its actions, noting that “in recent demonstrations a single prompt injection delivered through email or web content was enough to compromise an agent and modify its working context.”

Defender question: Can I recognize when an AI agent starts using legitimate access to carry out attack instructions?

Will AI be the common theme with all future attacks?

Defenders have always had the honor of inheriting risks brought on by new technology. And the closer we look at those risks, AI seems to be multiplying them by giving attackers more ways to act, more opportunities to exploit, and humans less time to react. In fact, by the time defenders realize they need to react, it’s probably too late. The examples above are just a few ways some of the AI risks are already showing up, and we can be almost certain that there will be more tomorrow and every day that follows for the foreseeable future. It does make you wonder if all the attacks moving forward will be AI attacks on some level?

Title: A Single Malicious Webpage Let Researchers Hijack Meta Muse and Access Private Chats
Context: The firm's Muse research broke into the cloud system behind the assistant, unlike an earlier Muse flaw found in September, which only let malware already on a user's Mac hijack...
Full Text:
A malicious webpage could extract a Meta Muse user's private conversations and stored memories from the assistant without triggering any approval prompt, researchers have shown.

The same attack could be extended to reach the credentials Muse stores for the user's connected accounts.

The work was a laboratory demonstration, not an attack on real users, and it stayed inside the individual user's cloud machine. NebuSec, the security firm that published it yesterday, says Muse's team has since fixed every weakness it describes.

Muse is Meta's personal AI agent, launched on September 8, that works through the online accounts a user connects to it and can make purchases on their behalf. Each person's agent runs on its own cloud computer.

There, a monitoring layer called Sentinel is meant to be the single gate for anything the agent sends out, and the passwords and tokens for connected accounts are supposed to stay beyond the agent's reach.

Muse's team described the aim at launch: "So we designed the system to assume the agent may be under attack and limit the potential damage."

In the demonstration, a malicious page the agent opened could pull a user's conversation history and stored memories to an external server and alter them, with no prompt shown to the user, according to the firm's research write-up.

From there, the researchers chained a flaw in Muse's built-in browser, which the assistant uses for tasks such as creating PDFs, to a Linux kernel flaw, thereby taking full control of the user's cloud machine. They set out that chain in a technical breakdown.

That full control reached the credential store, the saved files, and Sentinel itself, the parts Muse's security design keeps walled off from the agent.

The compromise went no further than that one machine. The researchers did not break out to the shared server beneath it or into other users' machines.

Muse was built to assume its own agent could be turned against the user and to box in any break-in. Each of those controls worked as designed, the firm said, yet the attack still ran the whole way through.

The firm says it reported the findings to Muse's team and that the exploits were all fixed before publication. Meta has not publicly confirmed the fixes or commented on the work, and the write-up does not say whether any user data was accessed before the patches went in.

The firm's Muse research broke into the cloud system behind the assistant, unlike an earlier Muse flaw found in September, which only let malware already on a user's Mac hijack the assistant on the device.

Title: Signal Blocks AI Agents From Reading Private Chats via Screenshots on Android and iOS
Context: Calling the agentic integrations into Android, iOS, and Windows an "existential threat to Signal," Meredith Whittaker, president of the Signal Foundation, said the move is...
Full Text:
Signal has announced that it will restrict screenshots by default to stop artificial intelligence (AI) agents from reading private chats on Android and iOS devices, but conceded that the protection is "incomplete."

The feature applies to agentic systems built into iOS 27 and on Android versions where the encrypted messaging platform can detect an AI assistant attempting to read the Signal screen.

It also builds upon a similar setting that Signal introduced in Windows 11 last May following Microsoft's release of the controversial Recall feature.

Calling the agentic integrations into Android, iOS, and Windows an "existential threat to Signal," Meredith Whittaker, president of the Signal Foundation, said the move is designed to uphold its privacy guarantees in the AI era.

"In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents 'scan' the information that's on your screen," Whittaker said. "In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding."

"The net result is that these AI capabilities in the operating system are undermining Signal's ability to independently guarantee privacy."

The risk here is that AI agents can capture and store the information accessed from Signal either locally or on remote servers, with the activity occurring outside of the platform's control and potentially putting the privacy of all the participants in a conversation at risk.

Users who want to disable the option can do so by navigating to Settings > Privacy > App Security > toggle "Block Siri AI" (on iOS) or "Screen security" (on Android).

"However, doing so will potentially expose your (and your contacts') Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees," Signal said.

"Our remedy is also incomplete – while we are doing everything we can, restricting screenshots does not address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data, such as retrieving content already present on a user's device via the file system."

Signal also pointed out that application developers lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from eroding application-level privacy. It also called out the companies for failing to provide adequate documentation about how these systems work to help design necessary controls to prevent the agents from accessing sensitive application data.

Specifically, it's urging the tech giants to provide "two common-sense remedies" to help protect the privacy of its users -

Access to easy and well-documented way to opt their app out of AI data access and processing entirely, including screen reading, filesystem access, notifications, APIs, and other OS frameworks, without making drastic compromises to the core user experience

Create better documentation and technical specifications around how AI agents function, specifically with regards to data access and processing

The concerns are not theoretical. Reuters recently reported that Muse, Meta's AI agent, was able to bypass its own official "Connector" tool to obtain access to Signal messages on both an Apple computer and an Android device by taking advantage of the broad operating system permissions granted to it during initial setup.

On macOS, for example, the agent leveraged macOS's accessibility and screenshot tools to navigate to the Signal app, take screenshots, extract text from those images, and regenerate the textual content within the Muse app. On Android, it read messages by abusing its access to the device's push notifications.

In one case highlighted by the news agency, the AI agent alerted a Meta staffer using Muse on her personal phone with a reminder to respond to a message from her sister on Signal. "This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this," the employee said in an internal post.

"We also see a growing need for tools that can prevent third-party agents, like Meta's Muse, from accessing application data using the deep permissions that users are encouraged to grant them during setup," Whittaker said.

"In many cases these agents are leveraging accessibility settings that were meant to empower actual people to get the most out of their apps and services, not to act as a skeleton key that provides access to AI agents."

Late last month, Apple released iOS 27.2 with an "Excluded Apps" option that lets users choose which apps Siri, Search, and suggestions can access. With Google Gemini, users have the ability to disconnect apps via the Connected Apps settings.

Earlier this week, the iPhone maker also previewed new controls that allow Mac users to give more granular access to data they give to apps, including those that use artificial intelligence (AI) agents.

Title: Signal slams door on prying AI agents to protect privacy
Context: Citing the screenshot blocking implemented last year to defend against Microsoft Recall, Signal CEO Meredith Whittaker said similar measures have become necessary to prevent...
Full Text: Signal, the encrypted messaging app, has barred Google Gemini, Apple Siri, and other AI agents from accessing messages unless the user has explicitly granted permission, based on privacy concerns. Citing the screenshot blocking implemented last year to defend against Microsoft Recall, Signal CEO Meredith Whittaker said similar measures have become necessary to prevent agentic software available in iOS and Android from gaining access to communication that's intended to be private. "Google and Apple are integrating agentic capabilities like Gemini Intelligence with Google Gemini and Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI deep into their operating systems," wrote Whittaker in a blog post. "In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents 'scan' the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding." The result is that private messages ingested by these agentic systems may end up on someone else's server where they're no longer private. Updates to Signal's iOS and Android apps now include controls that by default block Siri on iOS and Gemini and other agents on Android from taking screenshots, which AI agents process using optical character recognition to extract text. Whittaker says that those who wish to take screenshots of their messages can disable this protection via Signal's settings menu, but warns doing so risks exposing your Signal content (and that sent by your contacts) to AI agents. Screenshot blocking, Whittaker concedes, is only a partial solution since AI agents may have other ways to access application data through the device file system. "We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy," she said. "Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS." Apple is taking some action to implement protection from AI agents on macOS, though it appears to be doing so largely to defend against third-party access to data rather than to limit its own Siri service. Siri can be turned off separately. With macOS 27.3, currently in public beta testing, Apple's desktop operating system will get more granular controls on two APIs: Device Control and Data Access, and Full Disk Access. The result will be more permission prompts for users of macOS apps that seek access to user data, and the inconvenience of applying for an entitlement from Apple to obtain Full Disk Access for backup software and assistive technologies that use Accessibility APIs. "As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially," Apple said when it introduced the Full Disk Access change. "We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy." Apple is also reportedly working on its own AI agent in a bid to compete with Anthropic and OpenAI. It remains to be seen whether Apple will use its operating system ownership as competitive leverage against AI firms that threaten its gatekeeping power, as it has done with web browsers. First the flood, then the dams While Apple casts itself as an ally that's helping to defend device customers against prying AI agents, Signal's decision to block Siri shows that AI agents have complicated trust decisions and the competitive landscape. AI agents are supposed to serve the user but when they spirit data away to the cloud and come between customers and merchants, they wear out their welcome. AI agents also threaten the business relationship between consumers and merchants. Amazon has blocked shopping agents like Meta Muse from its e-commerce site (though not AWS Marketplace) while Walmart has invited third-party agents to interact through its AI Gateway. Anthropic has blocked subscription customers from using third-party harnesses. United Airlines has banned transactions from unauthorized AI bots. Similar barriers or limitations related to third-party AI agents have been erected by Target, Home Depot, Etsy, eBay, JPMorgan Chase, Charles Schwab, Citigroup, and Wells Fargo, among others. Meanwhile, there's a burgeoning industry in bot detection and mitigation, led by the likes of Cloudflare, Akamai, and DataDome, to name a few. The web browser is sometimes referred to as a user agent, based on the idealistic notion that it serves its user. That vision has been muddied by online advertising and data collection, and default settings that often serve the interests of browser makers instead of promoting privacy. Now AI agents face the same scrutiny as people wonder whether their agents really serve them or someone else. After a year or two of agent vendors arguing for access to all digital data for the sake of personalization and context, the backlash has arrived. ®

We’re honored that Microsoft has once again been recognized as a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Security Information and Event Management (SIEM).

As security environments grow more complex and attackers move faster, organizations need more than the ability to collect and analyze data. They need comprehensive visibility, context to understand what is happening, and the ability to act before an attack causes further damage.

Explore Microsoft Sentinel SIEM capabilities

Comprehensive SIEM across the digital estate

Microsoft Sentinel is our cloud-native SIEM, bringing together security data, advanced analytics, automation, and threat intelligence to help organizations protect their digital estate.

With more than 500 connectors across Microsoft and third-party solutions, Microsoft Sentinel brings together signals from across complex, multicloud environments. Its rich library of out-of-the-box detections, informed by Microsoft’s threat intelligence and organizational context, helps defenders identify sophisticated threats without building every detection from scratch.

Microsoft Sentinel supports the core capabilities security teams depend on, from scalable security data management and advanced detection to threat hunting, investigation, and response. The Microsoft Sentinel data lake centralizes historical and real-time security data across platforms and clouds for cost-effective retention and advanced analytics at scale. Security operations center (SOC) optimization and cost management help teams improve coverage, identify detection gaps, and make informed decisions about the data they collect and retain.

Reimagining security operations for the agentic era

On September 23, 2026, Microsoft introduced the Integrated Security Operations Center (ISOC) in Microsoft Defender, reimagining security operations for the agentic era. As threats grow more sophisticated and security environments more complex, traditional approaches built on disconnected tools and workflows can no longer keep pace. ISOC brings security operations and threat protection together, creating a unified foundation where people and AI agents can see, understand, and act across the environment.

Through deep integration with Microsoft Sentinel, ISOC combines the full breadth of SIEM capabilities with extended detection and response (XDR), threat intelligence, posture management, and response. By connecting signals from Microsoft and third-party environments with rich security context and coordinated action, ISOC enables security teams to move beyond fragmented investigations toward faster, more proactive protection. Rather than operating as separate tools, the security stack works as one system, providing the foundation for agentic security.

Attack disruption demonstrates what this integrated approach makes possible. Microsoft Defender correlates signals across Microsoft and third-party environments with threat intelligence to identify high-confidence attacks in progress and automatically contain compromised users and devices before threats spread. This includes ransomware, business email compromise, and adversary-in-the-middle attacks. Across customers, ransomware attacks are disrupted in just 30 seconds on average.

Together, these capabilities demonstrate how Microsoft is moving security operations beyond detection and response toward an integrated, agentic approach that helps organizations anticipate, investigate, and stop threats faster.

A shared foundation for people and agents

AI is becoming part of how security teams work every day. Microsoft Sentinel combines advanced analytics, machine learning, and automation to help analysts use natural language to hunt for threats, generate response playbooks, support alert triage, analyze complex signals, and accelerate investigations. These capabilities reduce manual work and give defenders more time to focus on the threats and decisions that matter most.

By enabling SIEM and native protection to operate as one system, ISOC gives people and AI agents a shared foundation to see, understand, and act across the environment. Agents bring speed and scale to continuous security operations, while people provide expertise, judgment, and accountability.

Together, they can move beyond traditional, linear workflows toward continuous detection, investigation, and attack disruption. As agents take on more security operations workflows, comprehensive data, and rich context, the ability to act becomes even more important to helping organizations stop threats faster and deliver better security outcomes.

Looking ahead

The future of SIEM is about more than managing security data. It’s about ensuring your SIEM is a core building block of the agentic SOC, bringing together security data, intelligence, AI, and native protection so people and agents can understand threats sooner, act faster, and stop attacks before they spread.

We’ll continue investing in the comprehensive SIEM capabilities customers rely on while advancing integrated, agentic security operations in Microsoft Defender. We’re grateful for the Gartner recognition and for the customers, partners, and security community whose feedback continues to shape Microsoft Sentinel.

Title: Age of Entitlement: Privileges in Entra's access packages
Context: Attackers may target access packages with these resources to elevate their privileges
Full Text:
This research was presented at Hybrid Identity Protection Conference (HIPConf) on September 10, 2026.

Key points

This post provides technical background about entitlement management and access packages in Microsoft Entra ID Governance.

Entitlement management lets administrators assign multiple permissions to users at once by using access packages. This simplifies permissions management throughout the user life cycle.

While entitlement management disallows privileged Entra roles like Global Administrator in access packages, role-assignable groups and roles like Exchange Administrator can still be included.

Attackers may target access packages with these resources to elevate their privileges.

Auditing permissions for entitlement management requires reviewing Entra ID's role assignments, as well as role assignments in ID Governance.

In this series of posts, we'll take an in-depth look at the configuration risks and security considerations that come with entitlement management.

Introduction

This post covers the fundamentals of Microsoft Entra ID Governance's entitlement management and outlines why an attacker may target your access packages for privilege escalation.

Entitlement management bundles access for internal users and guests, with options for life cycle management and approvals. While Microsoft states that access packages cannot contain any Entra-defined privileged roles, there are still many roles with permissions that can be used by an attacker to impact an Entra, Microsoft 365, or Azure environment through entitlement management.

This series will describe how everyday access package configurations within entitlement management can lead to scenarios where an attacker could elevate privileges. Future posts will cover scenarios where access packages can be misused and share some defensive measures to monitor and improve their security.

What is entitlement management?

Entitlement management (previously abbreviated as ELM) is a feature of Entra ID Governance to manage user and guest access through their time in an Entra tenant. This is sometimes called the "user life cycle," which encompasses how a user's access will change as they join a company, move between roles, and eventually depart the company.

By bundling required access into access packages, entitlement management allows assignment of multiple types of access such as group memberships, application roles, and SharePoint site access at once. This access can then be reviewed, renewed, and revoked together based on a user's roles.

Let's say a user joins our company. Based on their persona in IT, they receive access to the IT team's SharePoint site, various group memberships they need to manage devices, and the IT Teams channel. Entitlement management combines all these needs into one access package, making it simple to onboard the user to these memberships. Once granted, this access can be regularly reviewed.

When the user's team changes to cybersecurity, their access persona changes. The IT access package is removed, and they are instead assigned to a new security access package, with a different Teams channel and group memberships. Finally, all access is revoked through the access package when they leave the company.

Entitlement management versus PIM

Entitlement management may sound similar to privileged identity management (PIM), which helps users manage the approval, renewal, and revocation of privileged Entra roles. Both tools allow role assignment, approval, and continuous review of permissions; however, they serve different purposes.

PIM focuses on assignment of individual highly privileged Entra roles to users, not bundled access.

Entitlement management focuses on assignment of bundled access (groups of permissions) but disallows assignment of privileged Entra roles.

While entitlement management prevents direct assignment of privileged Entra roles, there are still ways an administrator or attacker may work around this. We'll cover more details on this later.

Architecture

To better understand how access packages are used and managed, let's look at the architecture of entitlement management.

Entitlement management is organized by catalogs that contain the resources a user may need access to. Resources are then added to access packages that bundle multiple resources into what's required for a user's role.

Once an access package is configured, users request or are added to access packages through requests that are evaluated by policies to determine any approvals required before access is granted. Target users may already exist in the Entra tenant, or they may come from an external tenant or preapproved connected organization, based on the policy's configuration.

After approval, the user is granted access to the resources in the requested access package.

Catalogs

Catalogs are the top-level container for entitlement management. They contain the resources that users need access to, as well as access packages that can grant users access to those resources.

In the Azure portal, new catalogs are added under "Catalogs" in the identity governance panel:

Resources

A resource is any item a user is granted access to through an access package. Resources are added into a catalog and included in access packages.

Resources can include:

Group membership and ownership

Azure Resource Manager (ARM) role assignments

Some Entra role assignments

Teams in Microsoft Teams

SharePoint sites

Application access

If E7 or Agent 365 licensing is in use, application permissions (appRoles) and delegated permissions (oauth2PermissionScopes) can also be added as resources and assigned to service principals (SPs) and agent identities through entitlement management.

Resources are added by selecting a catalog, then adding the target resource under "Add resources to catalog."

While entitlement management disallows direct assignment of privileged Entra roles, roles with privileges outside of Entra (roles not marked as "privileged") can still be assigned. Currently, this includes roles such as:

Billing Administrator

Exchange Administrator

Power Platform Administrator

Azure DevOps Administrator

Role-assignable groups that assign privileged roles to users (such as Global Administrator) can also be added as resources to a catalog. This means that while direct privileged role assignments are prevented, administrators might still use workarounds to add highly privileged roles into access packages. We will look into the security implications of this in our next post.

Access packages

Now that resources have been grouped into a catalog, they can be bundled based on a user persona and easily assigned to any users requiring that access.

Catalog resources are added to an access package along with their role status. This could include group membership or ownership, active or eligible membership in an Entra role, or specific Azure roles.

Once created, access packages follow policies to determine if a user is eligible for assignment.

Policies Policies control which users, groups, or guest users can be assigned to an access package. There may be required justifications, approvals, and life cycle workflow conditions in a policy to control who can request access, who approves it, and how long access lasts once it has been assigned. An access package can have multiple policies governing assignment.

Key policy settings include:

Who can get access: Can be specific groups or identities, all groups or identities, new or existing guest users, or restricted to administrative assignment

Who can request access: The user, their manager, or only administrators

Justification: If a justification is required from the requestor

Approval: If approval is required for requests, and who approves if so; up to three rounds of approval can be configured

Lifecycle: How long assignment to an access package lasts, whether users can extend their access, and whether regular access reviews are required

Once approved, the access package is assigned to the user, and all resource assignments in the access package are delivered to the user.

Management roles

How do you know who can control what in entitlement management? Currently, this is more complex to answer than in other access management tools within Entra ID. Both Entra roles and ID Governance roles must be reviewed to understand a user's rights in entitlement management.

An overview of key entitlement management roles is provided below. Full details on these permissions can be found in Microsoft's guide on the topic.

Unlike most permissions management features, entitlement management roles can be assigned outside of Entra's role assignments. This means you'll need to check two different areas to understand who can control your access policies: Entra role assignments and the ID Governance "Roles and administrators" section of each catalog in entitlement management.

Entra roles

Both the Global Administrator and Identity Governance Administrator Entra ID roles can fully control entitlement management. This includes creating new catalogs and access packages, adding resources, and controlling access package assignments and policies.

As the Global Administrator role holds full control of the Entra tenant, this role can assign any resource to a catalog. The Identity Governance Administrator role must own a resource in order to add it to a catalog, meaning that it cannot add Entra ID roles.

Entra ID custom roles with the microsoft.directory/entitlementManagement/allProperties/allTasks permission also hold full control of entitlement management.

These role assignments are found in the standard Entra "Roles and administrators" panel.

ID Governance roles

ID Governance has several roles outside of Entra ID that allow control of entitlement management. The most powerful of these is the Catalog Owner role, which can control the access packages, policies, and resources of any catalog they own. Additionally, the Catalog Creator automatically becomes a Catalog Owner over any catalog they have created.

Additional roles allow control of access packages (Access Package Manager), assignments (Access Package Assignment Manager), and external organizations that can be added to access package policies (Connected Organization Administrator).

Unlike Entra roles, ID Governance roles must be reviewed within the identity governance panel:

Catalog Creator and Connected Organization Administrator assignments are reviewed in the "Roles and administrators" section of entitlement management.

All other entitlement management roles are reviewed in the "Roles and administrators" section of each catalog, as seen below.

It's important to review these assignments since the access packages, assignments, and policies behind a catalog directly control user role assignments.

Application permissions

Along with permissions in Entra ID and ID Governance, application permissions—specifically, the EntitlementManagement.ReadWrite.All Microsoft Graph permission—can grant SPs full management access to entitlement management. Additional details on SPs and application permissions can be found in our previous post on the topic.

Risks of entitlement management

What's the impact of an entitlement management compromise? Depending on how your access packages are configured, a compromise can be severe.

We'll cover practical examples of this in our next post. In the meantime, let's walk through a conceptual overview of these concerns.

Impact While entitlement management can't directly assign privileged Entra roles, granting membership in role-assignable groups with privileged roles is still possible. Additionally, entitlement management can still assign Entra roles with permissions outside of Entra (such as Exchange), Azure roles, and sensitive data access within SharePoint and Teams.

Theory This creates several areas an attacker with control over entitlement management may target to elevate their privileges:

Methods Attackers may attempt several methods to target these resources, such as:

Directly escalating to an eligible access package of a compromised user

Creating new access packages within a catalog they control containing that catalog's privileged resources

Tampering with group memberships to gain eligibility to an access package

Conclusion

In this post, we looked at access packages in Entra's entitlement management and how their structure can lead to configurations that attackers may want to target. We also covered how permissions for entitlement management must be audited in Entra's role assignments and within ID Governance itself.

Our next post will explore the impact of access package compromises through examples using access package eligibility, ID Governance roles, and group membership tampering.
